svg.aria-label: Diagram: what the Google Cloud IAM recommender measures across its 90-day observation window, which access-control systems it cannot see, why a policy insight and a role recommendation are different artifacts, and the limits on the new custom roles it will offer
svg.title: IAM Recommender: observed usage through one access-control system, in a bounded window
svg.text: It reports what was observed used, not what is needed. Those differ at the edges.
One access-control system, a 90-day horizon, and a documented refusal to guarantee no breaking changes.
What it actually measures
Permissions the principal used in the last 90 days. 90 days is the MAXIMUM observation period.
Usage counts directly (an API call) and indirectly (the console reading a setting to show it).
ML fills the gaps: co-occurrence in observed history, role definitions, and word embedding.
Trained on k-anonymised data with the user ID dropped, so partly on patterns beyond your org.
What it cannot see, and what Google says about that
Generated from ONLY IAM access controls. Not ACLs. Not Kubernetes RBAC.
Policy insights do not list permissions used by non-public, early access features.
The candour worth quoting: we cannot guarantee that our recommendations will never cause
breaking changes in access. It never removes a permission used in the last 90 days, but 90 days
is the whole horizon, so a quarterly job falls outside it.
Insight and recommendation are not the same artifact
For a basic role, the console permission list may omit what the principal needs, because some
services use basic roles to indirectly grant additional roles.
Role recommendations automatically account for this discrepancy. So apply the RECOMMENDATION,
never your own reading of the insight list.
And the limits on what it will offer
New custom roles: project level only, never folder or organization.
None offered if the org already has 100 or more custom roles, or the project 25 or more.
At most 5 new custom roles per project per day, 15 across the organization.
Take the predefined role and the principal keeps unused permissions. Take the custom role and
you maintain it. No option is both strictly least-privilege and maintained for you.
#48: do not revoke service agent roles UNLESS a role recommendation suggests it. And service
agents are the one case where a recommendation MAY increase access.
The first tool in this series that tells you what to remove. It is also measuring one of the
several systems that decide access, across 90 days, and it says so plainly.
